findings.title: Unbounded Recursion in readTable and readArray
findings.impact: A maliciously crafted AMQP frame containing deeply nested tables or arrays could cause a stack overflow, leading to denial of service. An attacker who can send AMQP messages to the client could crash it.
findings.evidence: The readTable() method at line 139 recursively calls readFieldValue() which can call readTable() again (line 181). Similarly, readArray() at line 237 recursively calls readFieldValue() which can call readArray() again (line 184). No recursion depth limit is enforced. A frame with tables containing tables containing tables N levels deep will exhaust the stack.
findings.recommendation: Implement a recursion depth limit by adding a parameter to track nesting level and throwing an exception when a maximum depth (e.g., 16) is exceeded. Alternatively, use an iterative approach with an explicit stack instead of recursion.

findings.title: Unbounded Memory Allocation via Length Field
findings.impact: An attacker can send a frame with a large length field to cause the client to allocate excessive memory, leading to OutOfMemoryError and denial of service.
findings.evidence: The readBytes() method at line 83 reads a 32-bit length prefix (line 86) and allocates a byte array of that size without any sanity check on the length. The check 'contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE' is insufficient - it permits allocation of up to 2GB arrays. Similarly, readTable() at line 142 and readArray() at line 240 read length fields without validation against a reasonable limit.
findings.recommendation: Add a configurable maximum size limit (e.g., 128MB) for individual fields/tables/arrays. Throw an exception if the declared length exceeds this limit. This prevents memory exhaustion attacks from malicious or corrupted AMQP frames.

findings.title: Weak Type Handling - Missing Validation for BigDecimal Scale
findings.impact: A malformed BigDecimal with an extreme scale value could cause problems in downstream code or resource exhaustion.
findings.evidence: At line 172-175, when reading a BigDecimal (type 'D'), the code reads an unsigned byte for scale without validation, then reads 4 bytes for the unscaled value. A scale of 255 combined with large unscaled values could create a BigDecimal with extreme precision requirements, consuming resources unexpectedly.
findings.recommendation: Validate that the scale value is within a reasonable range (e.g., 0-127). Consider also validating the unscaled value size constraints to prevent resource exhaustion from pathological BigDecimal values.
